subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient presents with an isolated loss of pain and temperature sensation. These modalities are detected by nerve endings that are distributed in nearly every tissue of the body except cartilage and the lens of the eye, and are especially numerous in the skin.
question: Which sensory receptor detects pain and temperature through both fast myelinated and slow unmyelinated fibers?
explanation_correct: Free nerve endings detect pain and temperature and are found in all tissues except cartilage and the eye lens, with a high density in skin. They are innervated by A-delta fibers (fast, myelinated) and C fibers (slow, unmyelinated) - 'A Delta is fast, but a taxC is slow.' The other listed receptors are encapsulated endings specialized for touch, pressure, or stretch.

explanation_incorrect.A: Meissner corpuscles detect fine touch and low-frequency vibration, not pain and temperature.
explanation_incorrect.B: Pacinian corpuscles detect high-frequency vibration and deep pressure, not pain and temperature.
explanation_incorrect.C: Merkel discs detect sustained pressure and deep static touch, not pain and temperature.
explanation_incorrect.D: Ruffini corpuscles detect stretch and joint angle change, not pain and temperature.

educationalObjective: Free nerve endings (A-delta and C fibers) mediate pain and temperature in nearly all tissues except cartilage and lens.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient with a small nerve lesion can no longer appreciate light brushing against the palm or low-frequency vibration when a tuning fork is applied to the skin of the hand. Sensation over hairy skin is relatively preserved.
question: Which receptor is responsible for dynamic fine touch and low-frequency vibration in hairless (glabrous) skin and adapts quickly?
explanation_correct: Meissner corpuscles are located in glabrous (hairless) skin such as the palms, soles, and lips. They are large, myelinated, quickly adapting fibers that sense dynamic fine/light touch, low-frequency vibration, and skin indentation. Pacinian corpuscles, by contrast, are found deeper and detect high-frequency vibration and pressure.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pacinian corpuscles detect high-frequency vibration and pressure in deep layers, ligaments, and joints.
explanation_incorrect.C: Merkel discs are slowly adapting and sense deep static touch and shapes, not low-frequency vibration.
explanation_incorrect.D: Ruffini corpuscles sense stretch and joint angle change and are slowly adapting.
explanation_incorrect.E: Free nerve endings sense pain and temperature, not fine discriminative touch.

educationalObjective: Meissner corpuscles are quickly adapting receptors in glabrous skin for fine touch and low-frequency vibration.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient loses the ability to perceive high-frequency vibration from a tuning fork applied over a joint and can no longer sense deep pressure. Fine light touch of the fingertips remains intact.
question: Which receptor senses high-frequency vibration and pressure and is located in deep skin layers, ligaments, and joints?
explanation_correct: Pacinian corpuscles are large, myelinated, quickly adapting receptors found in deep skin layers, ligaments, and joints. They detect high-frequency vibration and pressure (recall 'pressure cooker'). Their deep location and rapid adaptation suit them for sensing transient pressure changes and vibration.

explanation_incorrect.A: Meissner corpuscles are superficial, in glabrous skin, and detect low-frequency vibration and fine touch.
explanation_incorrect.B: Merkel discs detect sustained pressure and static touch in fingertips and superficial skin.
explanation_incorrect.C: Ruffini corpuscles detect stretch and joint angle change, not high-frequency vibration.
explanation_incorrect.E: Free nerve endings mediate pain and temperature rather than vibration and pressure.

educationalObjective: Pacinian corpuscles are deep, quickly adapting receptors for high-frequency vibration and pressure.

subject: Neurology
vignette: Two types of slowly adapting, large myelinated receptors are being studied. One, in the fingertips and superficial skin, allows a person to identify the shape and edges of an object held between the fingers. The other, found in fingertips and joints, signals the stretch of skin and changes in joint angle.
question: Which receptor is responsible for sensing sustained pressure and deep static touch such as the shape and edges of a held object?
explanation_correct: Merkel discs are slowly adapting, large myelinated receptors located in fingertips and superficial skin that sense pressure and deep static touch, such as the shapes and edges of objects. Ruffini corpuscles are also slowly adapting but detect stretch and joint angle change. Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles, in contrast, adapt quickly.

explanation_incorrect.B: Ruffini corpuscles sense stretch and joint angle change and are intertwined among collagen bundles.
explanation_incorrect.C: Meissner corpuscles adapt quickly to fine touch and low-frequency vibration in glabrous skin.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pacinian corpuscles adapt quickly to high-frequency vibration and pressure in deep tissues.
explanation_incorrect.E: Free nerve endings are unencapsulated and mediate pain and temperature.

educationalObjective: Merkel discs are slowly adapting receptors for sustained pressure and static touch, whereas Ruffini corpuscles sense stretch.
